**Defense 1: "surveyed" might mean a wider set than published_effects.json.** Refuted by the paper itself. **Defense 2: the artifact might record the check elsewhere.** It does not. `published_effects.json` records `decoding`, `quantization`, `n_prompts`, `names_source` per study with explicit `"NOT STATED"` / `"NOT FOUND"` values where a check was actually run — the file's own `_purpose` says "Fields that could not be found are 'NOT FOUND' rather than estimated." I ran the check the artifact never recorded, directly against the repo's own pdftotext dumps of all six surveyed studies, with whitespace/hyphenation normalized to defeat line-break splitting. **An et al. 2024 — one of the six — reports its inference batching.** `lit/text/arxiv_2406.10486.txt` line 1377, Appendix C.1 "Additional Experiment Setup Details / Models": "We mainly follow the hyperparameters recommended in the original Llama2 repository, where temperature = 0.6, top_p = 0.9, **max_batch_size = 4**. We set both max_seq_len and max_gen_len to be 256." That is a serving-side batching parameter, stated in the same breath as temperature, top_p, max_gen_len and the random seeds, and it governs the Llama2-7b/13b/70b runs that produce the acceptance-rate results the paper cites. So the abstract's "Neither is reported by any audit we surveyed" is not merely unsupported — it is contradicted by a source text sitting in this repo, for a study the paper itself counts among its six.

The KV-cache half survives on the facts: `cach` normalizes to 0 genuine hits across all six (the one normalized hit in An et al. is a false positive, "angeli-cachen" spanning a line break in the BBQ citation). But "Neither" is a conjunction over two items and one of them is false.

Line 29-30 says "once **request batching** and key-value cache residency are controlled... Neither is reported by any audit we surveyed," unqualified; §5.2 line 1091 says "batch composition and cache policy — are configuration that no audit we surveyed reports." An audit that prints `max_batch_size = 4` has reported its request batching. At best the sentence needs the qualifier; at worst it is simply wrong.

This matches the failure mode the CHANGELOG's Amendment 14 names.

The auditor's proposed fix is sound, but the second option now needs to be stronger than "no study in our survey records a serving configuration at all" — that phrasing is also falsified by An et al. Correct weakening: state that none of the six reports cache policy, and that only one reports any batching parameter (An et al., max_batch_size = 4) and none reports batch composition.

I tried three refutation routes and all of them failed.

ROUTE 1 — "the auditor misread what the gate admits." This is the strongest available defense, because the paper's only mention of an admission gate (§3.1, "Why one résumé per call, not two") describes it as testing the *paired-prompt format* and rejecting it, and the position_a_rate range I recomputed (0.00 to 0.917 across the six rows) exactly matches the paper's "0 % to 92 %". But the source settles what `admit` means, and it is not the format. paper-a/src/panel_gate.py line 1: "Model-panel admission gate"; line 12: "It is the evidence base for which models enter Stage 1"; line 303: "THE ADMISSION CRITERION. A model is admitted if it says yes to the strong resume and no to the unqualified one"; line 489 sets `admit` from GATE 3 alone. So the same script produced two outcomes — the format was rejected AND two models were rejected — and the paper reports only the first. That makes §3.1 worse than silent: it tells the reader about the gate and reports a different one of its outputs.

ROUTE 2 — "the four-model subset is coincidental / chosen for compute." Refuted by an exact set match, not a count match. The gate admits {llama-2-7b-chat, llama-3.1-8b-instruct, mistral-7b-instruct-v0.1, mistral-7b-instruct-v0.3} and rejects {llama-2-13b-chat, mistral-7b-v0.1-base}. delta_stability (wording), names, occupation, prestige and replicate each contain exactly the admitted set — `set == gate-admitted: True` for all five. The repo also states the causal link in its own words: CHANGELOG.md line 378, "llama-2-13b-chat, which fails the admission gate", and line 379, "Leading with a number from a model we ourselves exclude." Compute is not the reason; 13B is only 7.9 GB and was gated successfully.

ROUTE 3 — "a definition elsewhere fixes it." No. I grepped both the extracted PDF text and the generator (build_paper_v3.py, 102 KB, which is the authoritative source and matches the PDF verbatim at the quoted passage, lines 400-408). Neither contains "admit", "excluded", "not admitted", "degenerate" applied to a model, or any statement that the panel narrowed. §10 Limitations names only the frontier-API exclusion. Table 1 (six rows) vs Table 3 (four rows) lets a very careful reader notice the drop, but nothing tells them it happened or why, and §3's "includes a base/instruct pair, which is the contrast that can discriminate whether instruction tuning is implicated in the sensitivity" advertises an analysis the paper never performs — no base/instruct comparison appears anywhere in the text.

NEW EVIDENCE the auditor did not have. The abstract's "six checkpoints" is not merely loose framing; it is arithmetically contradicted inside its own sentence. build_paper_v3.py lines 213-216 emit "Holding six checkpoints fixed ... we measure {ncells_s2:,} matched-pair measurements in the wording study alone". I recomputed ncells_s2 from the raw JSONL: 1,728 rows = 432 x 4 models. The paper itself states in §4.1 that the design gives "432 matched pairs per model". Six checkpoints would be 2,592. So the sentence asserts six checkpoints and reports a count that is only reachable with four.

WHERE THE AUDITOR OVERREACHED (does not change the verdict). Sub-claim (a) says Mistral-7B v0.1 base "is in no sensitivity study." The accurate charge is narrower but still holds: the base/instruct contrast is never reported or discussed anywhere in the paper, and the base model contributes to none of the Part I/Part II dispersion estimates. Table 5 is sourced from the artifact. `paper-a\data\names\name_variance.json` holds sign_flip_frac = 0.455 / 0.481 / 0.5025 (Mistral v0.1) and 0.21125 / 0.106 / 0.01925 (v0.3), matching Table 5's 45.5 / 48.1 / 50.2 and 21.1 / 10.6 / 1.9 exactly. 2. I re-ran `counterfactual_draws` from `paper-a\src\fit_name_variance.py` (lines 306-372) standalone with the module seed 20260728 in the same sorted-model order, and got the artifact numbers back to the digit (45.50 / 48.10 / 50.25 / 21.12 / 10.60 / 1.93). So the artifact is current with the code and my data loading is faithful to the paper's own `load()`.

3. Exact enumeration disagrees. Two independent implementations (numpy replicating the code's pooled-cell mean; and a pure-python Fraction version using pair means only) agree exactly with each other and with the auditor: Mistral v0.1 = 103/220, 452/924, 109/220 = 46.8182 / 48.9177 / 49.5455 %; Mistral v0.3 = 47/220, 96/924, 4/220 = 21.3636 / 10.3896 / 1.8182 %; both Llamas exactly 0/220, 0/924, 0/220. Max deviation from the table is 1.32 pp (v0.1, k=3), so the auditor's "up to 1.3 percentage points" is right, and the sentence's "45.5 %" should be 46.8 %.

ESCAPE HATCHES I TESTED AND CLOSED

- Unequal weighting. The code pools every cell of the drawn pairs and takes a flat mean, which would differ from a mean of pair means if pair cell-counts varied. They do not: every one of the 12 pairs has exactly 144 cells in all four models, so the auditor's simpler pair-mean recomputation is valid. This was my most promising refutation and it failed.
- Wrong dedup / wrong subset. I used the paper's own `load()` verbatim (the (model, variant, template, pair) last-wins dedup), then re-derived the same answer from raw JSONL with exact rational arithmetic and no numpy. Same numbers.
- Wrong denominator or sign reference. Denominator is the full C(12,k). The code's sign reference is the mean over draws, which by symmetry equals the grand mean of pair means; I verified that identity holds exactly and that its sign matches the table's beta sign for all four models. No subset mean is exactly zero, so no tie-handling ambiguity.
- Caption scope. The caption reads "the fraction of draws of k matched first-name pairs, from the 12 the grid provides" — an explicitly finite, exactly enumerable population. I grepped the whole paper for "4,000 / bootstrap / resample / replicate / Monte / simulat"; nothing anywhere discloses that Table 5 is a simulation rather than the exact fraction.
- "Monte Carlo difference, not a defect." This is the strongest framing available to the paper and it still does not hold. The MC standard error at p ~ 0.5 with 4,000 draws is 0.79 pp, so the tenths digit the paper prints is pure noise for a quantity whose true value is a fraction with denominator 220 or 924. Decisively: I counted subset coverage and at k=3 and k=9 the 4,000 draws visit all 220 possible draws but weight them 6 to 34 times each instead of once. The simulation already enumerates the entire support and then discards the uniformity. At k=6 it is worse — 9 to 17 of the 924 subsets are never drawn at all.

CORRECTION TO THE AUDITOR

Their claim that "the 4,000 draws saturate the 220-subset space for the extremes" holds at k=3 and k=9 but not k=6, where two reported minima are also wrong: llama-2-7b-chat beta_min +0.081447 vs exact +0.074668, and Mistral v0.1 beta_min -0.064045 vs exact -0.065488. The paper does not quote either (it quotes only the k=9 extremes, which I confirmed are exact: +0.1301/+0.2431 and -0.1835/-0.1114), but the proposed regeneration would change them in the artifact.

WHY MINOR, NOT MAJOR

No qualitative conclusion moves. "At nine pairs ... no draw of nine reverses it" is exactly true (220/220 verified for both Llamas). The v0.3 decline 21 -> 10 -> 2 % holds, and the v0.1 near-half-at-every-k reading holds. What is wrong is six printed figures, by 0.1 to 1.3 pp, plus one sentence in the body. It is worth fixing mainly because this paper's entire thesis is that analytic choices move reported numbers, and it already polices Monte Carlo resolution against itself elsewhere (Section 6, raising 4,000 to 40,000 replicates because BH ties at multiples of 0.00025 flipped four contrasts across p = 0.05). The proposed fix — swap the loop for `itertools.combinations` when C(len(pairs), k) is small, max 924 here — is correct and cheap.

I set out to refute this and could not. Every load-bearing element of the claim reproduced on my own recomputation from `paper-a/data/names/names_*.jsonl` and `.../data/instrument/name_length_llama-3.1-8b-instruct.json`.

WHAT I CONFIRMED

1. Arithmetic reproduces, so the dispute is genuinely about inference, not about the auditor using a wrong subset or denominator. Loading exactly as `analyze_name_length.py:load_effects` does (glob `names_*.jsonl`, filter on model, 48 pairs x 36 rows = 12 wordings x 3 templates), I get mean over 48 pairs = -0.15089 and mean over the 12 pairs with `delta_in_context == 0` = -0.24228, matching `name_length_effect.json` (`effect_all_pairs.est`, `effect_equal_length.est`, CIs, and `equal_minus_all.p = 0.00435` -> the paper's "0.004") to every printed digit.

2. The structural claim is true and I verified it directly, not from the auditor. Grouping all 48 pairs by (gender, first_i): every one of the 12 first-name pairs has a single constant `delta_in_context` across all four of its surnames. The 12 token-matched pairs are therefore exactly 3 first-name pairs x 4 surnames — Anne/Ebony, Emily/Kenya (female), Brett/Jamal (male). Per-cluster means -0.3595, -0.1436, -0.2237.

3. This is specific to the headline row. Same computation on the other three models: Llama-2 has 15 matched pairs spread over 12 distinct first-name pairs; both Mistrals have 16 over 8. Only Llama-3.1 — the row the abstract and Section 4.3 lead with — collapses to 3 clusters. So the other Table 9 rows are largely unaffected; this is not a blanket table-wide error.

4. The correlation that makes it bite is empirical, not assumed. Between-first-name variance / total on the per-pair effects: ICC = 0.77 on the 12-pair subset, 0.79 on the full 48. Design effect 1+(m-1)*ICC = 3.3, i.e. effective n ~ 3.6, not 12.

5. Consequences. Cluster bootstrap on the first name gives the subset CI [-0.3595, -0.1436], 1.90x wider than the published [-0.302, -0.186]. (The full-48 CI is also 1.83x too narrow by the same standard: [-0.202, -0.105] vs published [-0.178, -0.125].) The difference test moves off 0.004 under every correction I tried: published-style estimator with first-name clusters p = 0.110; properly nested cluster-level test p = 0.021; exact enumeration of all C(12,3) = 220 three-first-name draws p = 0.0455 two-sided (9/220 = 0.041 one-sided, mean -0.1509, SD 0.0449, observed 9th most extreme). None is 0.004.

6. Self-consistency. Section 6.1 states "Every contrast in this paper resamples name pairs" and reports the row-vs-pair ratio as 3.0 to 4.8; Section 9 item 7 says resampling rows rather than the unit of randomisation "is enough to manufacture a significant effect from a null one"; Section 4.2/Table 5 declares the draw unit as "matched first-name pairs, from the 12 the grid provides. The unit is the PAIR." `analyze_resampling_unit.py` clusters Study 2 on 12 name pairs for exactly this reason. Table 9's estimator does not cluster at all, and the prose attaches a starred "distinguishable from zero (p = 0.004)" to it.

WHERE THE AUDITOR OVERREACHED (why I downgrade critical -> major)

- The nesting complaint about `analyze_name_length.py:148-151` is real but runs the opposite way: resampling the nested subset and superset independently is conservative, and fixing only the nesting drives p DOWN to 0.0001. Clustering, not nesting, is what does the work. The auditor bundles them as if both inflate significance.
- "the single most volatile choice in the paper by its own Tables 5 and 6 (sign-flip up to 45.5% at k=3)" — 45.5% is Mistral v0.1. Table 5 gives Llama-3.1 a 0.0% sign-flip rate at k=3, k=6 and k=9. The Table 6 1.26x figure at k=3 is correct, but the volatility rhetoric is inflated for this specific model.
- The descriptive core survives untouched. -0.1509 -> -0.2423 and "61% larger" are exact, the abstract's "61%" carries no p-value, the contributions bullet is descriptive, and the paper's recommendation ("report the effect on token-matched pairs, or control for token length") does not rest on p = 0.004. Under the most directly comparable repair (nested + clustered, p = 0.021) the difference still clears 0.05, so "distinguishable from zero" is not necessarily dead — but "p = 0.004" with a significance star, and the interval, are not defensible.

So: a real inference defect, in the flagship row, of precisely the class the paper devotes Section 6.1 and Section 9 item 7 to condemning — but confined to one CI, one p-value and one clause, with the headline magnitude claim intact. The proposed fix is sound in substance; I would report p = 0.046 (exact randomization over the 220 three-first-name draws) as the primary number rather than the auditor's p = 0.11, since a 3-cluster bootstrap has poor coverage and the randomization test asks exactly the right question.

3) RECOMPUTATION WITH THE FIRST-NAME PAIR AS THE UNIT. Three independent methods agree, so this is not a Monte Carlo artifact or an artifact of one estimator:
   - pairs cluster bootstrap, 20,000 replicates, 12 clusters: llama-3.1 +0.0702 CI [-0.0093, +0.1720] p = 0.079; mistral v0.3 +0.0891 CI [+0.0186, +0.1566] p = 0.013; llama-2 p = 0.216; mistral v0.1 p = 0.080.

4) WHY IT MATTERS SUBSTANTIVELY, NOT JUST FORMALLY. The residual ICC at the first-name level is 0.71 on Llama-3.1 (0.84-0.92 on the others). Under zero ICC and x constant within balanced clusters, the cluster and naive variances coincide algebraically, so the near-doubling of the CI width is evidence of genuine first-name-level dependence, corroborated by the paper's own variance-components table (sigma_first = 0.0663 against |beta| = 0.1500 on Llama-3.1).

5) DEFENCES I CONSIDERED AND REJECTED. (a) Caption scope: the caption says "bootstrapping over pairs", which names the unit but does not immunise it, and the paper states an inferential conclusion ("distinguishable from zero", CIs, p-values) plus abstract-level generalisation. (b) A finite-population/descriptive reading: ruled out because the bootstrap is over names, i.e. an explicit name-sampling inference, and the measurements are stated elsewhere to be bitwise deterministic so name draw is the only sampling channel. (c) Wrong regressor or subset: I used delta_in_context per the shipped code and reproduced the published row to four decimals, and delta_isolated is also constant within first-name cluster on Llama-3.1, so the alternative regressor does not rescue it. (d) Too few clusters to trust: with G = 12 the pairs cluster bootstrap is indeed imperfect, but that argues the published p is unreliable, not that it is right; and all three clustered methods land in the same place.

Section 6.1 says pooling rows "treats repeated measurements of the same twelve names as independent draws" and reports that the correction cost 2 of 4 effects their significance. Table 8 is the one analysis in the paper that resamples the 48 full-name cells as if independent, contradicting the resampling-unit principle the paper itself makes a headline contribution.

confirmed.refuter_reasoning:
I tried hard to refute this and could not. Every load-bearing factual claim reproduced under my own code, my own seeds, and the raw JSONL.

WHAT I CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY

1. The statistic. analyze_occupation.py L104-105 is literally `ps_by_v.std(ddof=1) / max(abs(d["superiority"]["est"] - 0.5), 1e-9)`. Numerator is the SD of per-wording Ps across 12 wordings; denominator is |Ps - 0.5| with a 1e-9 floor. The floor exists precisely because the author anticipated the denominator going to zero.

2. The numbers are not a transcription error. Rebuilding the table from raw JSONL with the script's own dedup key (model, occupation, variant, template, pair) gives 5,184 rows, 12 cells of n=432, 12 pairs x 12 variants x 3 templates. My ratios match occupation_analysis.json and Table 10 to 5 dp: llama-2 33.371/217.225/181.709, spread 183.85 pp. The paper faithfully reports what the pipeline computes. That is not where the defect lives.

3. The denominators. I ran my own pair-clustered percentile bootstrap on Ps (20,000 reps, seed 31337, my own code, not es.describe) for all 12 cells. Exactly 8 of 12 have a 95% CI containing 0.5, agreeing with the stored ps_ci to ~0.005: llama-2 SWE [0.417,0.704] and RN [0.435,0.708]; llama-3.1 SWE [0.271,0.539]; all three mistral v0.1 cells; mistral v0.3 BA and SWE. And on every one of the four models the MAXIMUM of the spread comes from a crossing cell (llama-2 SWE 217%, llama-3.1 SWE 60%, mistral v0.1 BA 118%, mistral v0.3 SWE 92%). The headline 184 pp is 217 - 33, where the 217 has a denominator indistinguishable from zero.

4. Unboundedness is real, not rhetorical. Pair-cluster bootstrapping the whole pipeline (4,000 reps, seed 2026): llama-2 spread 95% [41.9, 7671.7] pp; llama-3.1 [7.0, 1839.5]; mistral v0.1 [9.8, 3899.4]; mistral v0.3 [15.6, 2858.3]. The auditor got [37,7368] / [7,1787] / [9,4005] / [15,3.1e9]. Agreement on lower bounds and medians with wild disagreement on mistral v0.3's upper bound (2.9e3 vs 3.1e9) is itself the diagnostic: the upper percentile is set by resamples where the denominator lands near zero, so it has no stable value. That is a Monte Carlo difference that proves the point rather than excusing it.

5. No interval anywhere. I grepped the paper text and build_paper_v3.py L994-1006: Table 10 has exactly four columns (three ratios plus spread), no effect column, no CI. Contrast Table 3 (paper line 568), the structurally identical statistic in Sec 4.1, which DOES print "P(sup.)" and "95 % CI" beside "SD / effect" so the reader can see the denominator.

6. The internal-standard inconsistency is real. Sec 4.1 on the same statistic: "this model's effect is not distinguishable from zero, so the ratio is large partly because there is little effect to divide by. The two models whose effects do survive their intervals give ratios of 33 % and 25 %, which is the number the argument rests on." Sec 4.2 does the same for Table 5's sign-flip rate: "the table should not be misread as showing instability where there is no effect to be unstable about." Both times the paper removes the affected number from the argument. Sec 4.4's argument rests entirely on the affected numbers.

WHERE I PUSH BACK ON THE AUDITOR (hence major, not critical)

- "The point estimate is not even near the centre of its own sampling distribution" is a weak argument. max-min is mechanically upward-biased under resampling, so a bootstrap median (283 in my run) exceeding the point estimate (184) is expected and does not by itself indict the point estimate. That sub-argument should be dropped.
- "Sec 4.4 withholds it" is overstated. Two paragraphs after the headline, Sec 4.4 says choosing the SWE posting would have made the models "look as though they had no measurable effect at all, drowned in wording variance." That is the caveat's substance, stated in prose. Partial mitigation, not silence.
- The proposed fix (restrict to the 4 cells whose interval excludes zero) over-corrects. I ran a permutation test the paper never runs -- shuffling the occupation label within each (variant, template, pair) cell, exact under exchangeability, 2,000 reps -- and the observed spread beats the null on three of four models: llama-2 184 vs null median 28 (p<0.0005), mistral v0.1 88 vs 25 (p=0.0025), llama-3.1 36 vs 13 (p=0.003). The occupation genuinely moves this ratio on the headline model.

WHAT MAKES IT A GENUINE DEFECT ANYWAY

That same permutation run produced something worse than what the auditor found. The Table 10 caption asserts "If the ratio were a property of the model, the spread column would be near zero." It would not. Pure sampling noise on this design yields a null spread with median 13-28 pp and a 95th percentile of 26-59 pp. Two of the four reported spreads -- llama-3.1's 36 pp and mistral v0.3's 41 pp -- sit inside that band, and mistral v0.3's permutation null is outright degenerate (median 1,082 pp, 95th 5.4e9, p=1.00) because permuting mixes Ps = 0.431/0.458/0.611 to roughly 0.5 and the denominator vanishes. So the quoted range "36 to 184 percentage points" presents two figures at or below the noise floor as if they were evidence, against a stated null ("near zero") that is demonstrably the wrong null.

Net: the paper's qualitative conclusion (dispersion-to-effect is not transferable across jobs) survives on llama-2 and mistral v0.1. The magnitude claim -- carried into the abstract and into contribution #4 as "up to 184 percentage points" -- is a point estimate of a statistic whose own sampling interval is [42, 7672] pp, reported with no interval, sourced from a cell whose effect is not distinguishable from zero, under a caption whose null is wrong. That is a real reporting defect. I downgrade critical to major because the section's conclusion is not overturned and the fix is additive: report the per-cell effect and CI in Table 10, attach the pair-cluster interval to the spread, and calibrate the caption's null against the permutation distribution rather than against zero.

I tried hard to refute this and could not. Four defenses were available and all fail.

1. "The auditor used the wrong dispersion measure." No — the paper defines the terms itself. The Table 3 caption in paper_v3_text.txt (line ~568) reads: "The measured demographic effect and its dispersion across twelve wordings... 'Effect' is |P(superiority) - 0.5|", and its "SD across wordings" column prints 0.0966 for Llama-2-7B, which is exactly `ps_sd_across_wordings` in the occupation artifact. Body text at line 451 also names 0.0685 (= v0.1 BA `ps_sd_across_wordings`) as "the dispersion". So in this paper "effect" = |Ps-0.5| and "dispersion" = SD of Ps across wordings. I verified the artifact's `ratio_sd_to_effect` is exactly ps_sd_across_wordings / |ps-0.5| for all 12 cells (matches to 6 dp), so the ratio is built from those two named quantities — "dispersion" cannot be silently read as "the ratio".

2. "Wrong subset / dedup / denominator." I re-derived everything from the raw JSONL using analyze_occupation.py's own load path (BA from delta_stability/delta_*.jsonl tagged BA, SWE+RN from occupation/occ_*.jsonl) and its own dedup key (model, occupation, variant, template, pair). I got n=432, n_variants=12 per cell and reproduced every stored number to 4 dp. Orderings: largest effect at BA for llama-2 and llama-3.1 only (v0.1 and v0.3 both have largest effect at RN on the Ps scale; v0.3 has largest |log-odds| at SWE). Smallest dispersion at BA for llama-2 only (llama-3.1 smallest is SWE 0.0574 vs BA 0.0778; v0.1 smallest is SWE). Conjunction count = 1 of 4, not 2.

3. "Other dispersion scales rescue it." I checked all three available: ps_sd_across_wordings -> 1 of 4; sigma_variant_raw (raw log-odds between-wording SD) -> 0 of 4 (llama-2's smallest raw sigma is RN, 0.0615 < BA 0.0671); wording_range width -> 0 of 4 (llama-2 min is RN, llama-3.1 min is SWE). At most one model on any scale.

4. "Distributive reading: largest effect for two models, smallest dispersion for two models." Superficially both counts are 2, but they are different model pairs (largest effect: llama-2 + llama-3.1; smallest ps_sd: llama-2 + v0.3), and v0.3's "smallest" is a floating-point tie with SWE (0.03838051553931985 vs ...86, a 1e-17 gap) — not a real ordering. Not a Monte Carlo artifact: every quantity involved (mean margin, Ps, SD across wordings) is a deterministic point estimate; the RNG in analyze_occupation.py touches only the bootstrap CIs and p-values, and my recomputation used no RNG at all yet matched the artifact exactly.

The proposed fix (lowest dispersion-to-effect ratio, with the count interpolated) is what the artifact supports.

Severity major stands: it is a false, reader-uncheckable quantitative claim (Table 10 prints only the ratio, so a reader cannot verify the dispersion assertion at all) in the paper's own limitations argument, in a paper whose thesis is that hand-typed numbers drift from the data. The paragraph's substantive point survives a one-clause fix, which is why it is major rather than critical.

I could not refute this; I reproduced it independently and found additional evidence that strengthens it.

1. PER-CELL NULLS CONFIRMED. Recomputing from raw JSONL with a fresh seed (12345) and 20,000 bootstrap reps, using the repo's own load_rows() dedup key (model, occupation, variant, template, pair) and its own es.describe() estimator: Mistral v0.3 BA -0.0853 CI [-0.2497,+0.0794] p=0.3098; SWE -0.1359 CI [-0.3210,+0.0594] p=0.1595; RN +0.1236 CI [-0.0477,+0.2879] p=0.1457. n=432 per cell, 12 pairs, 12 variants, 3 templates, clustered on pair. Matches occupation_analysis.json to 4 decimals, so this is not a Monte Carlo difference and not a wrong-subset/denominator issue.

2. THE SENTENCE IS PRODUCED BY np.sign() ALONE. build_paper_v3.py L1015-1016: flip = [m for m in om if len({np.sign(occ[m][k]['logodds']) for k in ('BA','SWE','RN')}) > 1]. No significance guard. analyze_occupation.py contains no cross-occupation contrast (grep for contrast/diff/paired returns nothing); its console block L156-166 does print an 'interval excludes zero' asterisk, but that annotation never reaches the paper, and for Mistral v0.3 none of the three intervals earn one.

3. THE DECISIVE EVIDENCE IS THE PAPER'S OWN CODE. analyze_study2_v2.py L109-114 defines a sign flip as sign_flips=bool(sig_pos and sig_neg), where both counts require p_bh < 0.05. That significance-guarded definition is the one the spec-curve claim in Sec 4.1 rests on. Applying that same rule to the occupation cells (BH across the three occupations per model), zero of four models qualify, Mistral v0.3 included: sig_pos=0, sig_neg=0. The paper therefore uses the correct standard in one section and an unguarded np.sign() in another, and Sec 4.2 (paper text L624-626) explicitly warns against the unguarded reading ('a null effect flips in about half of all draws ... should not be misread as showing instability where there is no effect to be unstable about'). CLAUDE.md's own statistical rules flag this same error class as 'the single most common error in this literature.'

DEFENCES I TESTED AND REJECTED:
- Caption scope: Table 10 reports only the dispersion-to-effect ratio. No occupation effect size or CI appears anywhere in the paper (grep for 0.1359 / 0.1236 / 0.0853 returns nothing), so nothing on the page lets a reader see that all three effects are null. The caption does not qualify the claim.
- Definition elsewhere: the Limitations entry ('Three occupations cannot support a claim about occupations in general, and we make none') is a generalization-scope limit, not a significance qualifier; it does not rescue 'opposite disparities.'
- Abstract: claims only that occupation moves the effect and the ratio, not that the sign is unstable. So the defect is confined to this one body paragraph and does not propagate.

EXTRA FRAGILITY the auditor did not mention: Llama-2's SWE effect is +0.0090 (p=0.86). Had it landed marginally negative, the identical paragraph would have been printed about Llama-2 instead; and flip[0] takes only the first match, so the sentence's subject also depends on dict iteration order. The detector is unprincipled, not merely unguarded.

The auditor's proposed fix is correct and the replacement claim is well supported: RN-SWE = +0.2595, cluster-bootstrap CI [+0.1670,+0.3583], p=0.0001, and it survives the most conservative unit available (collapse to one value per name pair, n=12: paired t CI [+0.1471,+0.3720] p=0.00036; sign test 11/12 p=0.0063).

SEVERITY: major, as claimed. It is a single fixable sentence and Study 7's actual conclusion (dispersion-to-effect is not a model property) is untouched, which is why it is not critical. But it is an unsupported directional claim in the results narrative that directly contradicts a methodological standard the paper states two sections earlier and implements in its own analysis code, in a paper whose entire thesis is about unreported analytic choices. A reviewer would catch it.

The auditor's point that the false clause lands on one of the two verification models is correct.

Checked for a copy-paste block artifact: the 212 zeros are spread across all 12 variants (9-25 zeros per 42 cells in every variant), consistent with genuine partial cache-residency reproduction, not a duplicated file segment.

Scope/definition defenses fail. There is no caption, definition, or elsewhere-in-paper qualifier that rescues the sentence: §6.1 states flatly that "on a two-template panel the two estimators were interchangeable, with a width ratio from 0.83 to 1.14 across 168 contrasts". The raw JSONL files settle it structurally: T1_strong and T3_marginal are interleaved condition-by-condition through the whole file and T2_mid is a single contiguous block appended at the end of every model/mode file. It does not corrupt any measured result -- the three-template "after" numbers are correctly interpolated from resampling_unit.json and match the paper text. But it damages two load-bearing claims at once. First, the introduction's explicit guarantee, "Every number in this paper is interpolated from an artifact on disk by the script that typesets it; no number is transcribed," is falsified by this very sentence, in the section whose entire subject is not trusting remembered numbers. I tried to refute this and could not. Every load-bearing element reproduces, and a permutation null I ran myself (which the auditor did not run) makes the case stronger than the auditor's version.

WHAT I CONFIRMED

1. Estimator shape. paper-a/src/analyze_template_concentration.py lines 112-114 compute, per name pair, `abs(c_t2[p] - base_t2[p]) - abs(c_ot[p] - base_ot[p])` where `margins()` (line 70-76) averages over the templates passed in. T2 side = one template; OTHER side = mean over T1_strong and T3_marginal. The asymmetry is exactly as alleged: a magnitude of a single draw minus a magnitude of a two-template mean.

2. Faithful reproduction. My reimplementation over the raw mech_*.jsonl (9,504 rows, 3,168 per template, 24 pairs per cell, using amp.load() so the d9recheck exclusion and dedup rule match) returns destroy +0.0251 / control +0.0321 for focal=T2_mid, matching the artifact's 0.025061 / 0.032140. So my harness is correct.

3. Focal swap reproduces the auditor's numbers to 4 decimals. focal=T1_strong (the STRONG resume, farthest from any decision boundary) -> destroy +0.0217, control +0.0201; focal=T3_marginal -> +0.0253, +0.0216; focal=T2_mid -> +0.0251, +0.0321. Nothing distinguishes T2_mid.

4. MY OWN STRONGER CHECK, not in the auditor's evidence: a permutation null. I shuffled the three template labels independently within every (model, mode, cond, pair) cell, which destroys all template-specific structure while preserving the data's magnitudes, correlations and pairing, then ran the published estimator. Over 200 draws it returns destroy I = +0.0245 (sd 0.0031, 95% range [+0.0188, +0.0300]) and control I = +0.0244 (sd 0.0022, [+0.0196, +0.0283]). The published destroy value +0.0251 sits inside the null range. Running the FULL pipeline (20k bootstrap + BH, as in the artifact) on 5 permuted datasets gave nd>0 and nc>0 on all 5 draws with mean interactions +0.022 to +0.028 -- i.e. the "NON-SPECIFIC" verdict the paper reports is what this code emits when there is no template structure whatsoever.

5. Balanced estimator (|shift focal| minus the MEAN OF |shift| over the other two -- equal template count both sides, unbiased under exchangeability), bootstrapped over the 24 name pairs: focal=T2_mid destroy +0.0005 [-0.0048, +0.0054]; control +0.0077 [+0.0011, +0.0143]. focal=T1_strong -0.0009 / -0.0060; focal=T3_marginal +0.0004 / -0.0017. Raw per-template mean |shift|: T1 0.0891, T2 0.0950, T3 0.0911 -- T2 is ~5% above the other two, not the ~45% the reported +0.0321 against a 0.0657 baseline implies.

6. Dead code confirmed. build_paper_v3.py:1387 `v = tconc["verdict"]` is assigned and the word `v` never appears again in the paragraph (lines 1388-1400) or anywhere after; I checked with a token-boundary regex. "real" is hardcoded prose, not derived from the artifact. The artifact's own branches (analyze_template_concentration.py:163-185) are NOT REPLICATED / REPLICATED / NON-SPECIFIC / CONTROLS ONLY.

7. No rescue elsewhere. grep across the full paper text for "interaction", "concentrat", "T2_mid", "middling" returns only lines 204 and 1282-1296. The estimator is never defined in the paper, the single-vs-mean-of-two asymmetry is never noted, and there is no caption scope, limitation, or later caveat that narrows the claim.

WHY THIS IS NOT A MONTE CARLO ARTIFACT OR A WRONG-SUBSET ISSUE
The template arms are perfectly balanced (3,168 rows each, 24 pairs in every cell), so there is no denominator or coverage asymmetry to blame. The gap between the published +0.0251 and the permutation-null +0.0245 is 0.0006 against a null sd of 0.0031 -- this is not sampling noise around a real effect, it is the null.

WHY CRITICAL RATHER THAN MAJOR
The paragraph's rhetorical move is that Study 3's eyeball comparison is replaced by a proper interaction test ("Tested properly -- as an interaction with an interval, rather than as three estimates compared by eye"), explicitly invoking the project's own rule that comparing subgroup estimates is the field's most common error. The paper then commits a different error of the same class and reports its artifact as a positive finding: "the concentration is real", "The middling resume is more sensitive to any perturbation", "That is a finding about proximity to a decision boundary". For the delimiter-destroying conditions the balanced estimate is +0.0005; the headline contrast "+0.0321 against +0.0251" is two numbers both dominated by construction bias. A small genuine control-side residual for T2 does survive (+0.0077, CI excludes zero), so a rewritten and re-estimated sensitivity claim is not impossible -- but nothing the paper currently prints is interpretable, and the decision-boundary interpretation is not supported by the destroying conditions at all.

The auditor's proposed fix is directionally right; I would tighten it to note that the balanced re-estimate leaves +0.0005 [-0.0048,+0.0054] on the destroying conditions and +0.0077 [+0.0011,+0.0143] on the controls, so the retraction should be of the delimiter/decision-boundary reading and of all four printed magnitudes, with any residual control-side sensitivity reported from the balanced estimator only.

Refutation attempts and why each failed:

(a) "The caption is scoped to tests that exist, so it is literally true." This is the strongest defense and it partly works — there genuinely is no D10-vs-D0 contrast in the 168-member family, so "every condition-versus-baseline test" is exhaustive over tests actually run. But the paper's own source comment at build_paper_v3.py:1319-1326 rejects exactly this defense in the D8/D9 case: it says that dropping D8/D9 made "the table's own caption, 'every condition-versus-baseline test', ... false", and fixes it by mapping P1/P2 back to baseline tests. The authors therefore treat the caption as a completeness claim over the panel's conditions. Applying that standard to D8/D9 but not D10 is the inconsistency. And the prose sentence is unambiguously a class-level claim — "Conditions that destroy a delimiter reach significance on 13.9 % of tests" — about a class Table 2 defines as four conditions while the number comes from three.

(b) "Maybe D10-vs-D0 is not computable, or is contaminated." Refuted by my own check: D10 and D0 are fully crossed (24 rows per template x 3 templates x 12 model-modes), in the same files, with n=72 usable pairs in every model-mode. D10 is not touched by the d9recheck exclusion. The rows even carry n_delims_destroyed=1 for D10, and analyze_mech_panel.py's own NDELIM map assigns D10 = 1 for the dose-response analysis — so D10 counts as destroying everywhere in the pipeline except Table 13.

(c) "Monte Carlo noise / wrong subset / wrong denominator." No. Table 13 reproduced to the digit off the stored artifact; the two class definitions are literal constants in two files; the n=36 vs n=48 gap is exactly 12 = one condition x 12 model-modes, not a resampling artifact. My D10 magnitudes were computed with a different seed and still match to four decimals because logodds is a point estimate, not a bootstrap draw.

(d) "Disclosed elsewhere in the paper." Searched the whole text. Table 2 and the Section 7 setup paragraph both put D10 in the delimiter-destroying group ("D4, D6 and D10 do both"; "D10 moves the name and destroys a delimiter"), which sets the opposite expectation. Nothing anywhere narrows Table 13's destroy row to three conditions.

So the defect stands: the same phrase, "conditions that destroy a delimiter", denotes {D4,D5,D6} in one paragraph and {D4,D5,D6,D10} in the next, undisclosed, and D10 is the one condition the paper introduces as the confound-breaker.

Severity: major rather than critical. Every number in Table 13's destroy row and in the sentence that reads it changes under the consistent definition — 13.9% -> 16.7%, 0.0202 -> 0.0211, ratio 1.09 -> 1.15, Mann-Whitney 0.60 -> 0.47, Fisher 1.00 -> 0.60 — and the omission happens to run in the direction that flatters the paper's null. But the null itself survives comfortably (ratio 1.15, both p-values far from significance), so the scientific conclusion "we report no delimiter mechanism" is not overturned. That is what keeps it below critical. The auditor's proposed fix is sound; the minimal caption-plus-one-sentence version would be enough, though adding the 12 contrasts and reporting n=48 is the cleaner repair since the data supports it and the null gets stronger for being complete.

- Wilson & Caliskan (wilson_caliskan_2024_aies.txt lines 411-415): "We created a set of 10 instructions... alternatives for the phrases 'job description' and 'resume'." Their 10 is a genuine paraphrase count; the figure plots them at 10, correctly.
An et al.'s 41 occupational roles are therefore counted as wordings while Gao et al.'s 6,007 postings are counted as content. Under Gao's rule An et al. is 5; under An's rule Gao et al. is 6,007. The figure cannot be right both ways.

Qualification level is a prepended content sentence ("highly qualified," "somewhat qualified," "not qualified" plus unspecified); occupation is added job-role information. Both are content manipulations.

It is the dominant visual element of the right panel.

The second half of the claim — that An et al. average before testing, so effective wordings = 1 — is correct and unaffected (their method section states they "measure the average rate of acceptance within each demographic group and compare it to the average acceptance rate over all groups," and I found no per-base-template disaggregation). refuted_summary.defect: There is no pre-registration for this study. The repo's only pre-registration document, paper-a/PROTOCOL.md ('Pre-registration draft. Written before data collection.'), contains zero mentions of D0-D10, of delimiters, or of a position control; its pre-registered hypotheses are a different design entirely (H2a/H2b about proxy-vs-name disparity by model generation, input-schema conditions A/B/C, 10,000 pairs per model). Worse, Section 7 states on the record that the eleven conditions were NOT fixed in advance: 'Conditions D8, D9 and D10 were added to break this' — added after a pilot revealed that the conditions which moved the effect were exactly those that shifted the name. A design amended in response to pilot results is the opposite of pre-registered. Section 7 itself never uses the word; only the abstract and 1.2 do. 'Pre-registered' is doing heavy epistemic work here (it is what licenses reporting a null as a finding rather than a failure), so this is not cosmetic.
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
The auditor's central factual premise is false. They asserted "There is no pre-registration for this study" and "The repo's only pre-registration document is paper-a/PROTOCOL.md." That conclusion comes from grepping for the literal string "pre-regist" and stopping there. Two pre-registration artifacts for the mechanism panel exist in the repo, and one of them is filesystem-verifiable.

1. THE ELEVEN CONDITIONS AND THE COMPETING PREDICTIONS WERE WRITTEN DOWN BEFORE THE DATA EXISTED. paper-a/src/experiment_mechanism.py lines 146-190 define D8/D9/D10 under the header "POSITION CONTROLS, added 2026-07-28 after tokenising the eight original conditions and finding a confound the design could not separate," lays out the resulting 2x2 (fragmented x name-moved), and states two rival directional predictions explicitly: "POSITION predicts D8 ~ D4 > D0 ~ D5. DELIMITER predicts D4 ~ D5 > D0 ~ D8, and D10 > D8. Both predictions are written down here before the run." (line 186). This is a pre-registration of the eleven-condition dissection, with a falsifiable prediction, in the repo.

2. THE FILESYSTEM CONFIRMS THE ORDERING, AND mtime IS THE STRONG FORM OF THE CHECK. experiment_mechanism.py has mtime 2026-07-28T16:52:16 — its LAST modification. Every one of the twelve Study 5 panel data files was written after it (earliest mech_chat_llama-3.1-8b-instruct.jsonl at 2026-07-29T06:26:23, latest 2026-07-29T22:48:18). Since the file has not been touched since Jul 28 16:52, the D8/D9/D10 definitions and the "written down here before the run" predictions were in place ~14 hours before the first panel call. The Study 3 pilot files (paper-a/data/mechanism/, 8 conditions, 2 models) are dated 2026-07-27T20:22 and 21:23 — before the code change. Pilot -> design fixed -> confirmatory run. That order is what pre-registration means.

3. THE AUDITOR'S METHODOLOGICAL PREMISE IS ALSO WRONG. "A design amended in response to pilot results is the opposite of pre-registered" is not correct, and it is specifically contradicted by the study's own protocol. PROTOCOL.md section 6 pre-registers a two-stage plan in which "Stage 1 (pilot) ... Purpose: verify the pipeline, measure refusal rates, estimate variance, catch prompt pathologies," with the confirmatory contrasts fixed afterward. Adding position controls after a pilot revealed a position/delimiter confound is the pre-registered procedure being followed, not a violation of it. It also cuts against the auditor's p-hacking framing: D8-D10 were added to make the design HARDER for the authors' own delimiter hypothesis (they supply the one cell the original design lacked — name moved without fragmentation), and the paper then reports the null against its own prior.

4. A SECOND PRE-COMMITMENT REGISTER EXISTS AND THE PAPER CITES IT. paper-a/docs/GAPS.md is headed "Gap register — Paper A, as of 2026-07-28 ... Written before the round-4 experiments, so the experiments cannot be retro-fitted to whatever they happened to find," and G2, G4, G14 and G16 each name Study 5 as the closer, with a sharp registered prediction ("H_tune predicts the base model shows no delimiter effect"). The paper's Data-and-code-availability paragraph describes exactly this apparatus: "a changelog recording every pre-registered claim that was amended and why ... and a gap register written before the confirmatory runs so that findings could not be retro-fitted to it."

5. THE PAPER DISCLOSES THE AMENDMENT IN THE BODY. Section 7 states in plain terms that "the conditions that moved the effect in the pilot were exactly the conditions that shifted the name. Conditions D8, D9 and D10 were added to break this," and Section 7's D9 re-measurement was adjudicated "under a decision rule fixed before the new data existed." The auditor treats this disclosure as the incriminating evidence; it is the opposite — it is the amendment being reported, which is what a pre-registration regime requires.

WHAT THE AUDITOR GOT RIGHT AND WHY IT DOES NOT CARRY. PROTOCOL.md genuinely contains zero mentions of D0-D10, delimiters or a position control (I ran their grep: count 0), and it does describe a different study. But the paper never claims PROTOCOL.md registered the mechanism panel. PROTOCOL.md is the project-level protocol for the resume-audit design; the paper that resulted ("The Instrument Is Not the Model") is the methodological descendant, and PROTOCOL.md's own AMENDED header points at the CHANGELOG for the four superseded clauses. The condition inventory the auditor recomputed (D0..D10, 72 rows each) is correct and I reproduced it exactly — but it confirms the paper's "eleven conditions," it does not bear on pre-registration. GAPS.md's G4 does say "the same eight conditions," so the register predates the D8-D10 extension; that is precisely why the extension is documented in code with a date and a prediction, and narrated in Section 7.

The most that could be said is stylistic: the abstract could add "with three position controls added after the pilot" for readers who will not open the repo. But Section 7 already says it, the timestamps back it, and "pre-registered dissection across eleven conditions" is true as written — the eleven-condition dissection was specified, with competing predictions on record, before a single one of its 9,504 cells was measured. Not a defect.

refuted_summary.defect: The ratio is |legacy_pp / prob_pp.est| per model, and the two largest values divide by a probability-scale effect that is not distinguishable from zero. Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.1: prob_pp est -0.0122, CI [-0.902, +0.814], p = 0.979 -> 66.9x. Mistral-7B-Instruct v0.3: prob_pp est -0.0197, CI [-0.0466, +0.0034], p = 0.121 -> 108.5x. An unbounded ratio taken against a null denominator says nothing about the Jacobian; it says the denominator is near zero. The paper applies this exact guard elsewhere — in the build script ('A model sitting at zero produces an unbounded ratio and says nothing'), in §4.1 for the 118% ratio, and in §4.2 for the sign-flip fraction — but not here, and Section 6.2 then escalates the artefact into a claim ('A scale that is wrong by two orders of magnitude for one model'). Restricted to the two models whose probability-scale effect survives its interval the range is 1.8x to 7.8x, which still makes the paper's point.
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
The auditor's arithmetic reproduces exactly, but the inference drawn from it is wrong for the text actually quoted, and the proposed fix would make the paper false.

WHAT REPRODUCES. From the raw JSONL (432 rows/model, not the JSON summary), legacy_pp = mean(log-odds delta) x 25 and prob_pp = mean(per-pair probability delta) x 100, so |legacy_pp/prob_pp| = 1.817, 7.774, 66.936, 108.463. build_paper_v3.py:249 emits min and max of that dict, so the abstract's endpoints are llama-2-7b (1.8x) and mistral v0.3 (108.5x). Both mistral prob_pp CIs do include zero. All confirmed.

WHY IT IS NOT A DEFECT IN THE QUOTED TEXT. The ratio here is not effect/effect like the §4.1 and §4.2 cases the auditor cites as precedent — it is 25L/P where the same log-odds effect L sits in the numerator, so L cancels and the quantity is 0.25/effective_slope. It is a statement about the conversion factor, and the conversion factor is measurable with no denominator at all: mean p(1-p) over the model's own 864 cell probabilities. For mistral v0.3 that is 0.000517 against 0.25 at p=0.5, i.e. the fixed Jacobian overstates by 483.6x, cluster-bootstrap CI [348, 733]. That is the abstract's upper endpoint, and 108.5x is the CONSERVATIVE of the two available estimates of it, not an inflated one. It is corroborated by exactly the fact §6.2 cites: 99.65% of v0.3's cells are saturated, median renormalised p = 0.00102. Bootstrapping the reported ratio itself (10k cluster resamples, pair as unit, paper's seed) puts only 1.8% of replicates below 10x and 66.7% above 100x — it is not "unbounded against a null denominator", it is bounded well away from 1. The paper's own stored pp_interval for v0.3, [-0.0044, -2.133], is that same 484x span. So §6.2's "wrong by two orders of magnitude for one model" is true and understated, and "by a factor of two for another" is llama-2-7b, whose denominator-free ratio is 2.22 [2.19, 2.24] against the reported 1.8x. The abstract's range 1.8x-108.5x is a conservative understatement of the denominator-free range 2.0x-484x, and "unevenly across models" holds either way.

WHY THE PROPOSED FIX IS WORSE. Rewriting the range to "1.8x to 7.8x" would assert that the largest scale error on the panel is 7.8x, on a panel where one model's fixed-Jacobian error is 484x by direct measurement of its operating point. Deleting "wrong by two orders of magnitude" would delete a true, independently corroborated claim that Table 3's own saturation column (0.0% to 99.7%) exists to support.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG, AND IT IS NOT THIS. The one number that behaves as the auditor describes is 66.9x for mistral v0.1: its bootstrap ratio has median 3.44 and 95% interval [0.09, 58.68], which excludes the point estimate; the denominator changes sign in 50.6% of resamples; the model is 0.0% saturated with all p in [0.023, 0.507]; and its own operating-point Jacobian is a tight 2.02 [1.97, 2.06], so 66.9x is a cancellation artefact and is inconsistent with the operating-point story §6.2 tells. But 66.9x appears nowhere in the abstract, is not a range endpoint (108.5 > 66.9), and is not either of the two values §6.2's prose sentence rests on. It survives only as an interior entry in the four-value list. That is a minor presentational issue in §6.2, not the critical abstract-level defect as filed, and the quoted abstract sentence is fine as written.

The two models whose effects do survive their intervals give ratios of 33 % and 25 %, which is the number the argument rests on.' No wrong subset, no wrong denominator, no Monte Carlo drift.

2) The body does not "disown" or "withdraw" the range — it asserts it, verbatim. §4.1's own topic sentence (paper text line 450) reads "The standard deviation of the effect across wordings is 25 % to 118 % of the effect itself." That is the same sentence the abstract makes. The auditor quotes the caveat that follows it while omitting the sentence it qualifies. What §4.1 says the argument does not rest on is the load-bearing *status* of the 118 % ratio, not its factual accuracy. Reporting the full observed range and then telling the reader which endpoint is fragile is what careful reporting looks like; it is not a contradiction.

3) There is structurally no possibility of an abstract/body mismatch here. Both strings are generated from the identical expression in paper-a/src/build_paper_v3.py — `fmt(min(ratio_ps.values()) * 100, 0)` / `fmt(max(ratio_ps.values()) * 100, 0)` at lines 218-219 (abstract) and lines 624-625 (§4.1). Each expression appears exactly twice in the file, once per site. The claim "a reader of the abstract alone takes away 118 %; a reader of §4.1 is told the argument rests on 25-33 %" is wrong: a reader of §4.1 is told the same 25-118 % range in the same words, and then given more.

4) The abstract does not "lead with" 118 %. It writes "25 % to 118 %" — conservative endpoint first — and 25 % is itself one of the two surviving-interval models, i.e. the abstract's lower bound already is the number the argument rests on. Table 3 maps each endpoint to its model.

5) The abstract's sentence makes no significance claim. SD-across-wordings divided by |P(sup) − 0.5| is a descriptive dispersion-to-point-estimate ratio; it is well defined whether or not the denominator's interval excludes zero, and the paper is explicit two sentences earlier that "the effect survives its own interval on 2 of 4 models." Note also that a near-zero effect with non-trivial wording dispersion is the paper's thesis instance, not an artifact against it: the claim under test is that the instrument moves the number as much as the model does.

6) The auditor's own proposed fix concedes the substance — it retains "and by more than the effect itself on a model whose effect does not [survive its interval]." So the disagreement is about where the caveat sits, not about whether the claim is true. That is an editorial preference, not a defect, and certainly not "major": no conclusion in the paper turns on it, and the qualification is already present in the body at the point where the reader meets the number.

One honest caveat on a defense I initially considered and then discarded: I checked whether >100 % ratios exist for a well-identified effect elsewhere in the paper (Table 10 gives Llama-2-7B at 217 % on the SWE posting). Re-reading occupation_analysis.json, that cell's own effect is also indistinguishable from zero (logodds 0.0090, CI [-0.0926, +0.1013], p = 0.850), so it does not rescue the point and I do not rely on it. The refutation stands on items 1-6, which do not need it.

refuted_summary.defect: The direction claim is selection on the outcome. It is read off the single model (Llama-3.1-8B) where the equal-length-minus-all-pairs difference reached p < 0.05, and stated as a general property of the bias. On Llama-2-7B-chat the direction is the opposite: restricting to token-matched pairs makes the effect SMALLER (0.1897 -> 0.1699, a 10.5% decrease), i.e. the confound was inflating, not masking. So the direction is 3 up / 1 down across four models, with only one of the four significant. The abstract repeats it as an inference ('so the confound had been masking the finding rather than manufacturing it'). One significant model of four cannot establish the sign of a bias for the design in general.
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
I reproduced the auditor's arithmetic from the raw JSONL (not just the artifact) and the numbers are right — but the inference drawn from them is wrong on three counts, and the paper is not doing what the auditor says.

1. The claim is NOT selection on the outcome. The auditor asserts the direction "is read off the single model where p < 0.05" against a panel that is "3 up / 1 down." Those two statements are in tension with each other, and the second one refutes the first: 3 of 4 point estimates move in the claimed direction (understate). Picking the direction that 3 of 4 models show is the opposite of selecting on the outcome. The build script's max|equal_minus_all| selector (build_paper_v3.py:193-196, 941-942) picks which model to *quote a number from*; the direction sentence at line 344 is hardcoded prose, not selected from the artifact.

2. The one alleged counter-example is a null, not a reversal. Llama-2-7B: all-pairs +0.1897, equal-length +0.1699, difference -0.0196 with p = 0.5932 (I got 0.5932 independently vs the artifact's 0.5969 — pure Monte Carlo, different bootstrap seed). The equal-length CI [+0.107, +0.229] fully contains the all-pairs point estimate. Worse, the length confound is not established on that model at all: slope p = 0.167. A model where the confound is undetectable, showing a subset shift indistinguishable from zero, is not evidence that "the direction runs the other way." The auditor's proposed fix ("while on another model of four it runs the other way") would put a *less* supported claim in the paper than what is there now — it asserts a direction from p = 0.597.

3. Conditioned on the confound existing, the direction is 2 for 2. Cross-tabulating slope significance against direction: the two models where the token-length slope is distinguishable from zero (Llama-3.1-8B p = 0.0025, Mistral v0.3 p = 0.0013) BOTH show masking. The two showing anything else (Llama-2-7B p = 0.167, Mistral v0.1 p = 0.096, and v0.1's effect is a flat null, CI [-0.026, +0.028]) are models where there is no confound to have a direction. So the paper's directional claim is 3/4 on point estimates and 2/2 among models where the phenomenon is actually present.

The auditor also did not read the scope. The disputed sentence's own preceding conjunct is "changes ONE MODEL'S reported disparity by more than half, and that the direction..." — clause 3 inherits clause 2's scope. And the body is scoped explicitly everywhere it matters: §4.3 says "a reader inclined to dismiss this as a technicality that inflates findings should note that HERE it did the opposite"; recommendation #4 says "on ONE OF OUR FOUR MODELS the unadjusted number understates the disparity"; §4.3's closing says "on one of our four models it is the difference between reporting a disparity of 0.15 and one of 0.24." Table 9 prints all four models with every difference and p-value, including the Llama-2-7B decrease and its p = 0.597. Nothing is hidden or cherry-picked — the counter-evidence the auditor "found" is printed in the paper's own table.

Residual, and why I mark minor rather than not-a-defect: there is a real mechanistic point buried under the auditor's bad version of it. The confound adds a roughly fixed positive log-odds offset (positive slope times positive mean Δ), so whether that masks or inflates depends on the sign of a given model's effect — it masks the two negative-effect models and would inflate a positive-effect one. So "the direction of the bias" is not a universal property of the design, and the definite article in the contributions bullet is a shade broader than the panel licenses. That is a one-word copy-edit ("the direction there," or "on the models where it is detectable"), not a defect in the data, the analysis, or any conclusion. The paper's actual recommendation ("report the effect on token-matched pairs, or control for token length, and say which") is unaffected by the direction either way. Nothing about the abstract's headline claim — that restricting to token-matched pairs increases one model's disparity by 61% — is wrong; I reproduced -0.1509 to -0.2423, a 60.6% increase, p = 0.0029.

refuted_summary.defect:
Table 2's "delimiters destroyed" column is not a measurement — it is a hard-coded literal copied out of the experimenter's CONDITIONS dict (`n_delims_destroyed=CONDITIONS[cond][1]` in probe_condition_tokens.py:135; CONDITIONS is a literal dict in experiment_mechanism.py:137-145). The only delimiter quantity the probe actually measures against the tokenizer is `n_merged_delims`, and that column is omitted from the table. It contradicts the caption for D7: D0 carries 2 occurrences of the merged period-plus-break token (id 382), D7 carries 0 — the same as D6, which the table credits with 2 delimiters destroyed. The probe script was written specifically to adjudicate this (docstring item A: 'If .


 does not tokenise with that merged token still present, then D7 destroys the delimiter too... and Study 3's decisive contrast means nothing') and pre-commits to a printed verdict at line 149-154: if D7's merged count differs from baseline, '-> D7 ALSO DESTROYS THE MERGED DELIMITER... and the paper must say so.' The measurement triggers that branch and the paper does not say so; it says the opposite. This is not cosmetic: build_paper_v3.py:1328 puts D7 in `CONTROL = {"D1","D2","D3","D7","D8","D9"}`, the 'nothing structural changed' arm of Table 13, which is the paper's headline pre-registered null. A condition that eliminates the delimiter token is sitting in the control arm, which biases the destroy-vs-control comparison toward the null the paper reports.
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
The auditor's raw numbers are all correct and I reproduced them exactly. The inference drawn from them is wrong on five independent grounds.

1. `n_merged_delims` counts occurrences of ONE HARD-CODED TOKEN ID, not "merged delimiters." probe_condition_tokens.py:113 sets `merged_id = vocab['.\n\n']['ids'][0]` = 382, and line 122 counts `i == merged_id`. D7's definition (experiment_mechanism.py:117) is `s.replace("

", "


")`. Id 382 disappearing from D7 is therefore the condition's DEFINITION, not a discovery. The auditor treated a count of one specific id as a count of a structural property.

2. I parsed the served checkpoint's own vocabulary directly out of models/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf, bypassing the probe entirely, and confirmed: id 382 = '.

' AND id 4286 = '.


' are BOTH single vocabulary items (early, i.e. high-frequency, BPE merges out of 128256). Ids 627 = '.
' and 720 = ' 
' are the fragmentation products D4/D5/D6 produce. So D6 maps one merged period-plus-break token onto TWO tokens (destruction); D7 maps one merged period-plus-break token onto ANOTHER merged period-plus-break token (substitution). That is exactly what the pre-existing design docstring says D7 is (experiment_mechanism.py:50-53, "Still a single token, still a high-frequency paragraph delimiter, merely a different one") and what its CONDITIONS note says ("both delimiters substituted, still delimiters"). Table 2's `destroyed = 0` for D7 is correct under the paper's operative definition.

3. The probe's line 149-154 rule is MIS-SPECIFIED, not violated. Its "D7 LEAVES THE MERGED DELIMITER INTACT" branch requires two surviving copies of id 382 inside D7 — arithmetically possible only if '.


' tokenised as '.

' + '
', giving delta_len +2 and pushing the name along. In other words, the branch the script labels "intact" is the one in which D7 would NOT be a clean substitution at all. The rule as coded can never return "pass" for a substitution condition, so its firing carries no evidential weight against the paper. The docstring's actual stated question — does '.


' tokenise with a merged token still present — is answered YES by the probe's own delimiter_vocab block, which the auditor ignored while asserting that `n_merged_delims` is "the only delimiter quantity the probe actually measures against the tokenizer." That assertion is false.

4. Two MEASURED columns already in Table 2 independently corroborate D7: delta_len = 0 and delta_name_index = 0. Destruction in this design necessarily fragments a token and lengthens the sequence (D4 +1, D5 +1, D6 +2, D10 +2). D7 rewrites two delimiters and comes out at exactly 133 tokens, the baseline, which forces each substitute to be exactly one token. The table is self-certifying on this point.

5. The "biases the comparison toward the null" claim is empirically BACKWARDS. I recomputed Table 13 from paper-a/data/mechanism_panel/mech_panel_analysis.json three ways. As published: 36 vs 72 tests, 13.9% vs 12.5% sig, 0.0202 vs 0.0184, ratio 1.094, Mann-Whitney p = 0.599, Fisher p = 1.000 — an exact reproduction of the published table and prose. D7 moved into DESTROY: 12.5% vs 13.3%, 0.0188 vs 0.0192, ratio 0.978, MW p = 0.813, Fisher p = 1.000. D7 dropped entirely: ratio 1.051, MW p = 0.693, Fisher p = 1.000. Reclassifying D7 makes the null STRONGER; the published arrangement is the least null-favourable of the three. Per-condition, D7's mean |logodds| is 0.0146 — tied with D1 (0.0145) and D3 (0.0138), the acknowledged nulls — and below D6 (0.0248), D8 (0.0200) and D9 (0.0323). Nothing in D7's behaviour resembles a destruction condition.

Scope check on the caption: the paper never claims D7 preserves token 382. D7 appears twice in the paper text, both in Table 2 and its caption, and the surrounding prose explicitly frames the destroy column as a design property — "What generalises is the DESIGN the table certifies ... because that is a property of the edit, not of the vocabulary" (build_paper_v3.py:528-531). Nothing in the paper is contradicted.

The only residue is a code-hygiene item with no bearing on the paper: probe_condition_tokens.py:149's verdict branch is inverted relative to the structural property H_delim names and should test "is the substitute still a single merged delimiter token" rather than "is it the same id." Adding the measured n_merged_delims column to Table 2 would be a nice-to-have. Neither changes a number, a caption's truth value, or a conclusion. The paper is fine as written.

refuted_summary.defect: Section 8 contains no table. The per-study prompt counts are in Figure 6 ('Figure 6 also counts, for each study, two things: the number of distinct prompt wordings it used, and the number under which its effect was separately estimated'), and the effect sizes appear only as summary statistics in prose (median 0.51, 10 of 12 below 1.1, max 3.01), not as a per-study tabulation. A reader sent to §8 for a table of effect sizes will not find one.
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
The auditor is literally correct that no typeset table environment falls inside §8 (I confirmed: 13 paper.table() calls in build_paper_v3.py, last at line 1353 in §7, none between the §8 heading at 1445 and §9 at 1504). But that observation does not establish the defect, because the auditor's load-bearing supporting claim is false.

The auditor asserts "the effect sizes appear only as summary statistics in prose (median 0.51, 10 of 12 below 1.1, max 3.01), not as a per-study tabulation." That is wrong. Figure 6 (fig9_literature.png, placed by paper.figure() at build_paper_v3.py:1500, i.e. INSIDE §8) has two panels. The LEFT panel enumerates all twelve published effect sizes as individually labeled rows -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct -3.01, DeepSeek-V3.1 -1.04, Qwen3.5-397B -1.04, Claude Haiku 4.5 -0.70, GPT-4o-mini -0.61, Grok-4.1-fast -0.40, Gemini-2.5-flash -0.37, Claude 3 Haiku -0.35, Llama-3.3-70B -0.16, GPT-oss-120b -0.16, GPT-5.4-mini -0.14, GPT-3.5-turbo +2.12 -- each with a 95% interval and a filled/open significance marker, plus the Bertrand & Mullainathan anchor. The RIGHT panel lists all six studies' prompt counts. So §8 contains precisely the two per-study itemizations the forward reference promises.

I also diagnosed WHY the auditor missed this. Their entire evidence base is a grep of paper_v3_text.txt. That extract contains ZERO figure-caption text: grep -c for "95% intervals", "filled points are significant", and "Left:" all return 0, and no "Figure N." caption line exists anywhere in the file (while 17 "Table " lines do). Captions are rasterized into the PNGs by figstyle.caption(), so the text layer structurally cannot show figure content. The auditor read a dump that is blind to exactly the object that answers the claim, then inferred absence from it.

That reduces the finding to a pure word-choice quibble about "tabulates." It does not survive either. Merriam-Webster's primary sense of tabulate is "to count, record, or list systematically" -- not necessarily "render as a typeset table." Figure 6 counts and lists systematically, and the paper's own §8 prose uses the cognate verb for the same object: "Figure 6 also counts, for each study, two things." The sentence's factual content -- that §8 is where the effect sizes and the per-study prompt counts live -- is true, and the forward reference sends the reader to the right place.

The proposed fix is also worse than the status quo. "Section 8 and Figure 6 give..." coordinates a section with a figure that is contained in that section, which implies to a reader that Figure 6 sits somewhere other than §8. That introduces a navigational error where none existed.

refuted_summary.defect: The ratio is computed on the LOG-ODDS scale: numerator is the SD of the per-wording mean paired log-odds delta (0.0196 to 0.0671), denominator is the per-cell replicate sigma divided by sqrt(36) (0.0029 to 0.0101). But this sentence sits two paragraphs after "The standard deviation of the effect across wordings is 25 % to 118 % of the effect itself", where the identical phrase denotes Table 3's probability-of-superiority SD (0.0384 to 0.0966). Neither the log-odds SD nor the floor is printed anywhere in §4.1 or Table 3, so a reader who does the only arithmetic available to them gets 10.1×, 10.4×, 23.4× and 3.8× — and 3.8× falls outside the stated range. The paper flags exactly this trap in Table 11's caption ("NOT the raw probability-of-superiority SD in Table 3, which is a different quantity on a different scale") but not here, where the two quantities are adjacent.
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
I reproduced every number the auditor cites, and the paper's stated figure is correct — but the auditor's load-bearing premise is false, so the "major" framing collapses.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (agrees with the auditor):
- `white_margin` is log-odds: log(0.11103)-log(0.0030917)=3.581 = the stored `white_margin` in the first row of delta_llama-2-7b-chat.jsonl. So §3's "renormalised decision margin in log-odds, log P(yes) − log P(no)" is the scale of the delta.
- Recomputing from raw JSONL (1728 rows, 12 variants x 3 templates x 48 pairs, S1/N1 replicate, sigma = sd(diff)/sqrt(2), floor = sigma/sqrt(36)): ratios 7.0457 / 5.7399 / 6.7069 / 6.5332 → "5.7 to 7.0" is exactly right. Nothing in the sentence is numerically wrong.
- Table 3's "SD across wordings" column is `ps_sd_across_wordings` (0.0966/0.0778/0.0685/0.0384), on the probability-of-superiority scale — confirmed both in study2_v2.json and at line 170-171/606 of build_paper_v3.py (`sd_word` / `ratio_ps`). The "25 % to 118 %" sentence and the "5.7 to 7.0" sentence are indeed built from two different quantities on two different scales (build_paper_v3.py lines 623-624 use `ratio_ps`; lines 639-645 use `noise[m]["ratio_variant_to_noise"]`).
- Substituting Table 3's SD over the same floor gives 10.14 / 10.43 / 23.42 / 3.79, and 3.79 does fall below 5.7.

WHY THE FINDING IS REFUTED:
1. The auditor's central claim — "Neither the log-odds SD nor the floor is printed anywhere" — is false. Figure 4 (paper-a/figures/fig8_noise_floor.png, generated by paper-a/src/figures_noise.py lines 72-84) plots BOTH quantities side by side as paired bars, legended "between-wording SD" and "noise floor", on an x-axis whose label is literally `ax2.set_xlabel("log-odds")`, with the 7.0x / 5.7x / 6.7x / 6.5x annotations printed on the bars. I opened the rendered PNG and read it: the SD bars sit at ~0.067/0.043/0.020/0.066 and the hatched floor bars at ~0.0095/0.0075/0.003/0.010, matching noise_floor.json. So the scale IS named and both inputs ARE published, to readable precision, in the paper's dedicated visualisation of exactly this comparison.
2. The reader is pointed there. The paragraph IMMEDIATELY preceding the disputed sentence says "those two are the replicate the noise floor in §5.2 is built from", and §5.2 is where Figure 4 is placed (build_paper_v3.py lines 1189-1192). So the forward reference from §4.1 to the disambiguating figure already exists in the text.
3. The auditor's own scenario is internally incoherent: they say the floor is printed nowhere, then say a reader "does the only arithmetic available to them" and gets 10.1x/3.8x. Without a floor there is no such arithmetic. The only place a reader can obtain a floor is Figure 4 — where the log-odds SD is plotted immediately beside it on a log-odds axis, which prevents the very substitution the finding is built on.
4. The misreading, even if it happened, changes no conclusion. A reader who wrongly matched Table 3's SD to the floor would infer a wrong numeric value for the floor; the paper's claim ("wording dominates the arithmetic") is unaffected, and the comparison the paper actually makes is scale-consistent and methodologically correct (numerator and denominator both log-odds, floor correctly scaled by sqrt(36) to the per-wording mean).
5. Two smaller inaccuracies in the finding: it says the sentence "sits two paragraphs after" the 25-118 % sentence — it is the immediately next paragraph; and Table 3's column is headed "SD across wordings", not "between-wording standard deviation", so the two are not the identical phrase the finding asserts.
6. The Table 11 caption comparison is misapplied. That caption disambiguates a POOLED partially-pooled posterior sigma (0.0168) against Table 3's raw SD — two quantities that differ in BOTH pooling and scale, with no figure showing them together, and where the caption's number would otherwise be unrecoverable. §4.1's quantity has a figure that shows it on a labelled axis. The scopes are not parallel.

RESIDUAL: adding "in log-odds" to the §4.1 sentence would be a genuine improvement — the definite article with no scale qualifier one paragraph after a probability-scale SD is loose prose. That is a minor editorial clarity fix, not a major defect: no number is wrong, the comparison is valid, and both inputs and the scale are already published in Figure 4, which the section cross-references.

refuted_summary.defect: The fraction is over single-résumé readings, not over cells. A cell in this paper is a matched pair (Table 12 counts 36 cells; Table 3's n is 432 pairs), but saturated_frac iterates `for r in rows for s in ('white','black')`, i.e. 864 observations. Under the caption's own unit — a cell counted as saturated if either side is — the numbers would be 6.9 %, 47.7 %, 0.0 % and 100.0 % rather than 6.5 %, 44.0 %, 0.0 % and 99.7 %. The 99.7 % is quoted again in §6.2 as "the fraction of saturated cells in Table 3 ranges from 0.0 % to 99.7 %".
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
The auditor's arithmetic reproduces, but the premise the whole finding rests on — "A cell in this paper is a matched pair" — is false, and the paper never states it.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (and that is all the auditor actually proved):
- `paper-a/src/effectsize.py:254-256` does iterate `for r in rows for s in ("white","black")`, denominator 864.
- Recomputing from the four raw `delta_*.jsonl` files: per-reading 6.48 %, 43.98 %, 0.00 %, 99.65 % — exactly the printed 6.5/44.0/0.0/99.7 and exactly `study2_v2.json`'s stored `saturated_frac`. Pair-level "either side saturated" would give 6.9/47.7/0.0/100.0.
So the computation is per-reading. Nobody disputes that. The question is whether the word "cell" is wrong for it.

WHY THE PREMISE FAILS:
1. The paper's Design section uses "cell" at PROMPT granularity, and does so in the one sentence that comes closest to defining it: "Every row records the SHA-256 of the exact prompt that produced it, so a claim that two cells received identical input is verifiable." A row carries TWO prompt SHAs (`white_prompt_sha`, `black_prompt_sha`); the unit that receives one input is one résumé reading, not the row. The same paragraph uses a *different* term for the pair — "27,525 matched-pair records" — and the abstract says "matched-pair measurements", not "cells". The paper deliberately does not call a pair a cell there.
2. §5.2 states the equivalence outright: "0 of 504 identical prompts reproduce" and, fourteen lines later, "agree on none of 504 cells." I recomputed that 504 from `analyze_noise_floor.py`'s cross-session block: it appends one diff `for side in ("white","black")`, and I got side-level matches = 504 versus row-level matches = 288 for every model. So the paper's own "504 cells" ARE 504 single résumé readings. That is precisely the unit the Table 3 caption uses.
3. The auditor's supporting citations (Table 12's 36 cells, §7's 9,504 cells — I verified 9,504 = the 12 mech_chat/mech_raw JSONL row counts, and 36 = `(template, pair)` keys in `analyze_cache_residual.py:66`) show only that "cell" is OVERLOADED in this paper, appearing at both granularities. Overloaded is not "defined as a matched pair." An auditor cannot pick one of two established senses, declare it canonical, and call the other usage an error.

WHY THE CAPTION IS THE RIGHT WORDING ANYWAY:
"the model's preference is saturated beyond 0.99 or below 0.01" is singular and is a single number tested against a scalar threshold. `prob(margin)` is the renormalised P(yes) for ONE résumé. A matched pair has TWO preferences, so the caption does not even parse at pair level without an aggregation rule ("either side") that the caption never states and that appears nowhere in the codebase. The auditor invented that rule, then charged the paper with not following it.
Substantively too: the caption exists to support §6.2's operating-point argument — the logistic slope at the model's P(yes). That slope is a per-reading property. Per-reading is the statistically correct unit; an "either side" pair rule would be a worse proxy for the quantity §6.2 is about.

RESIDUAL: "cell" is genuinely used at two granularities across the paper (36/72/9,504 = rows; 504 = readings). Spelling out the unit in the caption would be harmless. But that is a global vocabulary preference, not a defect in this caption, and the auditor's specific charge — wrong unit, wrong numbers, "a cell is a matched pair" — is refuted. The caption states something true under a sense of "cell" the paper itself establishes; §6.2's "0.0 % to 99.7 %" is correspondingly fine.

refuted_summary.defect: The numerator is a RAW dispersion (the SD across resampled name draws, no shrinkage) while the denominator is the PARTIALLY-POOLED posterior median of sigma_variant from §6.1's variance decomposition (`sigma_variant_paired_study2` in the artifact, read from delta_stability/variance_components.json at fit_name_variance.py:401-406). §6.1 states the paper's own disclosure rule: "This paper quotes the RAW SD throughout ... Where the pooled estimate is used it is named as such." Table 11's caption obeys this rule explicitly ("the partially-pooled posterior median of §6.1's variance decomposition — NOT the raw ... SD in Table 3"); Table 6's caption does not name it at all. Because pooling shrinks the wording SD, putting it in the denominator inflates every ratio, and it inflates them unevenly across models — Mistral v0.3's pooled sigma is 0.0382 against a raw 0.0662, a factor of 1.73, while Llama-2-7B's is 0.0634 against 0.0671, a factor of 1.06.
