The defensible claim is not that null edits move the effect more than paraphrases, but that they move it at all.' If the two arms cannot be told apart, a null-edit control does not 'separate genuine paraphrase sensitivity from surface-form sensitivity' — it demonstrates that surface-form sensitivity exists at the same magnitude, which is a different and weaker justification. Section 9 is the paper's actionable deliverable, so a recommendation whose rationale its own Part I falsifies is a direct target for a hostile reviewer.
refuted_summary.why_refuted:
The auditor's numbers are right and the inference drawn from them is wrong. The defect rests entirely on reading "separates" in Section 9 item 2 as "shows the two arms differ in magnitude." That is not what the word means in this paper, and it is not what a control condition does.

(1) The paper establishes its own usage of "separate" four times before Section 9, always meaning deconfound / make independently estimable: line 303 "The last two columns are what the design needs to separate"; line 1149 "components separately estimable"; line ~1249 "separates true between-wording dispersion from the sampling noise"; and decisively line 1265, "The design separates two things our first pass confounded" — followed two sentences later by "They do not differ. Conditions that destroy a delimiter reach significance on 13.9 % of tests; conditions that change nothing structural reach it on 12.5 %... We report no delimiter mechanism." That is the paper explicitly reporting a null as the OUTPUT of a successful separation, in the same voice, four pages earlier. Under the paper's own consistent usage, Section 9 item 2 says nothing Section 4.1 contradicts. The nearby line "Only with those in place does a null on delimiters mean anything" makes the point flatly: a control's value is that it makes a null interpretable, not that it guarantees a difference.

(2) Section 4.1 is the worked demonstration of the recommendation, not its falsification. The joint model estimates sigma_semantic and sigma_null as distinct parameters with distinct posteriors — ratio_null_over_semantic medians 0.455 / 2.519 / 0.727 / 0.640, sign of the contrast flipping across models. The quantity the auditor quotes ("the posterior probability that the null arm exceeds the semantic arm") is only computable BECAUSE the null-edit control separated the two sources. Without the control there is no contrast to put a posterior on. "Indistinguishable" is the answer the separation returned, not evidence that no separation occurred. The placebo-arm analogy is exact: a placebo arm separates drug effect from placebo effect even in a trial that finds them equal — that finding is only reachable through the arm.

(3) On this panel the null-edit control also delivered a hard, non-null separation the auditor ignored. Section 4.1 notes S1 and N1 are byte-identical token sequences embedded in the null arm, giving a per-model noise floor; I confirmed in noise_floor.json that ratio_variant_to_noise = 7.046, 5.740, 6.707, 6.533 (the paper's "5.7 to 7.0"), and reproduced the replicate gaps from raw JSONL (|S1-N1| = 0.0138, 0.0012, 0.0030, 0.0076 against between-wording SDs of 0.018-0.087). So the control demonstrably separated genuine surface-form sensitivity from arithmetic noise by a factor of six.

(4) Item 2 makes no empirical claim about this panel to be inconsistent with. Items 3, 4 and 7 of Section 9 explicitly cite the panel's findings ("on one of our four models the unadjusted number understates the disparity by roughly a third", "a factor of three to five"). Item 2 pointedly does not — it states a prospective design affordance and its cost ("It costs one extra condition"). There is no falsifiable assertion there for Part I to falsify.

The auditor's proposed fix is longer, states a weaker claim, and buys nothing the current sentence gets wrong. At most this is a stylistic preference about a word a hostile skim-reader could misparse; the paper conditions that word four times first.
